findings.description: The EC2 user_data script exports a static AWS access key ID and secret access key in cleartext. User data is retrievable from the instance metadata service by anyone with access to the instance (including via SSRF) and is stored unencrypted in the instance description, leaking long-lived AWS credentials.

No metadata_options block is defined, so IMDSv1 remains enabled and tokens are optional. Combined with credentials placed in user data and a web server exposed to the network, this permits trivial credential theft via SSRF against 169.254.169.254.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the root EBS volume is created without enforced encryption at rest, leaving data on disk and in snapshots unprotected.
The bootstrap script installs and serves content over plain HTTP (apache2 with no TLS configuration) on an instance in a public subnet, transmitting traffic in cleartext.
The EBS volume is created without encrypted = true (the encryption argument is explicitly commented out), so the attached data volume and any snapshots taken from it are stored unencrypted.

The EBS snapshot is created from the web host volume without encryption configured (the source volume is unencrypted, so the snapshot inherits that state). Snapshot data, including any sensitive data on the attached volume, is stored unencrypted and can be exposed if the snapshot is copied or shared.

The security group allows inbound TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administrative access on the attached EC2 instance/ENI to the entire internet and enabling brute-force and exploit attempts against sshd.

Inbound TCP/80 is open to 0.0.0.0/0 with no corresponding TLS (443) listener, meaning traffic to the public-facing web host is served over unencrypted HTTP and is subject to interception or tampering.
The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, giving a compromised instance unrestricted outbound connectivity for command-and-control channels and data exfiltration.

The subnet sets map_public_ip_on_launch = true, so every instance launched into it (including aws_instance.web_host / aws_network_interface.web-eni) automatically receives a public IPv4 address, exposing it directly to the internet rather than keeping it behind a NAT or load balancer.

The subnet sets map_public_ip_on_launch = true, automatically granting public IP addresses to any instance launched in it and removing the network boundary that would otherwise limit exposure of workloads to untrusted networks.

The VPC is created without managing its default security group (no aws_default_security_group resource restricting all ingress/egress), so the implicitly created default security group remains available and allows unrestricted intra-group traffic and all egress.

A default route (0.0.0.0/0) is pointed at the internet gateway on the route table associated with both subnets, making them public subnets. Combined with the web host and network interface placed in these subnets, this removes any network segmentation boundary and directly exposes instances to the internet.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (no server_side_encryption_configuration block or aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration resource). Flow logs reveal internal network topology and traffic patterns and are stored unencrypted.
No public access block or bucket-level ACL/policy restriction is declared for the flow log bucket, so it relies solely on account-level defaults to prevent public exposure of network flow log data.
The bucket has no access logging configured, so unauthorized reads or deletions of the VPC flow log data cannot be detected or investigated.

Versioning is not enabled and force_destroy is set to true, meaning the audit-relevant flow log objects can be overwritten or the entire bucket and its contents destroyed without recovery, aiding attacker log tampering.
No bucket policy enforcing aws:SecureTransport is present, so objects can be retrieved over unencrypted HTTP connections.
